Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Six years ago, Tuan Nguyen was twenty feet up on a commercial roof when the industrial sealant rig ruptured. A thick, acrid cloud of solvent fumes surged upward, enveloping him in the late afternoon light. He remembered the exact moment the pressure valve gave way, the way the chemical mist caught the sun, and the sharp, burning taste in his throat. His Vivid Memory of that day remains exceptionally clear and detailed, his mind holding the cracked asphalt beneath his boots, the frantic shouts from the crew, and the sudden tightness in his chest. His memories of the frightening event play over and over like a film reel, but sometimes the experience returns to him as pure Emotion Without Image, a raw surge of suffocation that arrives without a single visual cue. What frightened him most was how quickly the solid world beneath him turned unstable, how the familiar materials and weather he had trusted for decades suddenly felt volatile. He had come to believe that the World is Dangerous, one where a single faulty valve or shifting draft could overwhelm him without warning. As weeks turned into months, Tuan’s days reshaped around the lingering presence of the exposure. He worked as a roofer, climbing ladders and navigating the familiar topography of his neighborhood, yet he Avoided Unfamiliar Places because he could not assess the danger there. A new job site with unfamiliar ventilation systems or unmarked chemical storage tanks made him hesitate at the edge of the property, his boots heavy on the metal grating. At home, he Could Not Relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, his shoulders remaining tight, his breath shallow. His Concentration wavered during conversations as he tried hard not to think about the trauma, quietly Suppressing Thoughts to keep the intrusive images from rising. He dwelled on how he used to be before the event, watching his own hands move more carefully over the materials, while now he felt he Could Not Rely on himself to make the same steady decisions. Alongside this quiet uncertainty, he never disagreed or asserted himself to avoid conflict, preferring the predictable rhythm of his wife’s routines. The specific triggers of that rooftop exposure took on a distinct rhythm in his daily life. When the wind shifted and carried Related Smells of tar, fresh paint, or solvent from a neighbor’s house, his breath caught. A Hospital or antiseptic smell, particularly the sharp clean bite of rubbing alcohol at a clinic, pulled him back to the urgent care visit that followed the incident, while the lingering odors on his own coveralls served as a quiet, persistent reminder. Nighttime and waking up in the dark became particularly potent; when the house settled and the overhead lights dimmed, the shadows seemed to gather, and he would lie awake, certain that the air itself might turn heavy again. What kept him from moving forward was a steady sense of Hopelessness, a conviction that his best days were behind him and that another exposure or a sudden failure of his body could undo him. He had come to believe that his own internal compass had shifted, leaving him uncertain even when the sky was clear. Now, at sixty-six, Tuan sits with his wife in the kitchen, listening to the refrigerator hum and the neighborhood cars pass. He comes to therapy because the quiet accumulation of avoidance has narrowed his life more than he anticipated. He still climbs onto roofs when the job requires it, but he scans the sky and the materials with a new vigilance, his memories replaying, his thoughts suppressed, his concentration fracturing as the scents drift too close. He is most afraid of losing his remaining independence to a sudden wave of that familiar, unplaceable fear, yet he is hoping that understanding the pattern of his experiences might finally allow him to breathe as though the air, once again, were safe.
